content: On the American continent, cutaneous and mucocutaneous leishmaniasis (CL and MCL) are caused by infections with various species of Leishmania parasites. Pentavalent antimonials remain the first-line treatment, but alternative therapies exist. However, their effectiveness and safety need to be reviewed due to limited availability. This study is an update of a Cochrane Review first published in 2009. The objective of this review was to evaluate the effects of treatments for American cutaneous and mucocutaneous leishmaniasis (ACML) in immunocompetent individuals. The review included randomized controlled trials (RCTs) that assessed single or combination treatments for ACML. Participants were diagnosed based on clinical presentation and confirmed Leishmania infection through smear, culture, histology, or polymerase chain reaction (PCR) on biopsy specimens. Comparators included no treatment, placebo, or other active compounds. The review included 75 studies, with 37 new studies added, involving a total of 6,533 randomized participants. Most studies were conducted in Central and South America in regional hospitals, local healthcare clinics, and research centers. The majority of participants were male, with a mean age of approximately 28.9 years. The most commonly confirmed Leishmania species were L. braziliensis, L. panamensis, and L. mexicana. The most frequently assessed treatments were non-antimonial systemic therapies, particularly oral miltefosine, and antimonials, especially meglumine antimoniate (MA). Three studies included moderate-to-severe cases of mucosal leishmaniasis, but none addressed diffuse cutaneous or disseminated CL, which are considered severe forms of the disease. Lesions were primarily ulcerative and located on the extremities and limbs. Follow-up periods ranged from 28 days to 7 years. All studies had a high or unclear risk of bias in at least one domain, particularly performance bias. None of the studies reported outcomes related to functional or aesthetic impairment, scarring, or quality of life. When compared to placebo, intramuscular meglumine antimoniate (IMMA) administered for 20 days to treat L. braziliensis and L. panamensis infections in ACML may increase the likelihood of complete cure at one year (risk ratio [RR] 4.23, 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.84 to 21.38; 2 RCTs, 157 participants; moderate-certainty evidence). However, the wide confidence interval includes the possibility of both increased and reduced cure rates. IMMA probably increases the risk of severe adverse effects, such as myalgias and arthralgias (RR 1.51, 95% CI 1.17 to 1.96; 1 RCT, 134 participants; moderate-certainty evidence). IMMA may have little to no effect on recurrence risk, but the confidence interval includes the possibility of both increased and reduced risk (RR 1.79, 95% CI 0.17 to 19.26; 1 RCT, 127 participants; low-certainty evidence). Oral miltefosine, given for 28 days to treat L. mexicana, L. panamensis, and L. braziliensis infections in American cutaneous leishmaniasis (ACL), probably improves the likelihood of complete cure at six months (RR 2.25, 95% CI 1.42 to 3.38; moderate-certainty evidence). However, it also probably increases the risk of nausea (RR 3.96, 95% CI 1.49 to 10.48) and vomiting (RR 6.92, 95% CI 2.68 to 17.86). Miltefosine may have little to no effect on recurrence risk (RR 2.97, 95% CI 0.37 to 23.89; low-certainty evidence), but the confidence interval includes the possibility of both increased and reduced risk (all based on 1 RCT, 133 participants). When compared to IMMA, oral miltefosine given for 28 days to treat L. braziliensis, L. panamensis, L. guyanensis, and L. amazonensis infections in ACML may have little to no effect on the likelihood of complete cure at 6 to 12 months (RR 1.05, 95% CI 0.90 to 1.23; 7 RCTs, 676 participants; low-certainty evidence). However, miltefosine probably increases the risk of nausea (RR 2.45, 95% CI 1.72 to 3.49) and vomiting (RR 4.76, 95% CI 1.82 to 12.46) compared to IMMA (moderate-certainty evidence from 3 RCTs, 464 participants). Recurrence risk was not reported. Oral azithromycin, given for 20 to 28 days to treat L. braziliensis infections in ACML, probably reduces the likelihood of complete cure at 6 to 12 months (RR 0.51, 95% CI 0.34 to 0.76; 2 RCTs, 93 participants; moderate-certainty evidence) compared to IMMA. Adding topical imiquimod to intravenous meglumine antimoniate (IVMA) for 20 days to treat L. braziliensis, L. guyanensis, and L. peruviana infections in ACL probably makes little to no difference to the likelihood of complete cure at 12 months (RR 1.30, 95% CI 0.95 to 1.80; 1 RCT, 80 participants; moderate-certainty evidence) compared to IVMA and placebo. One session of local thermotherapy to treat L. panamensis and L. braziliensis infections in ACL reduces the likelihood of complete cure at 6 months (RR 0.80, 95% CI 0.68 to 0.95; 1 RCT, 292 participants; high-certainty evidence) compared to MA. Adding oral pentoxifylline to IMMA to treat CL (species not specified) probably makes little to no difference to the likelihood of complete cure at 26 weeks (RR 0.86, 95% CI 0.63 to 1.18; 1 RCT, 70 participants; moderate-certainty evidence) compared to IMMA and placebo. The authors concluded that the certainty of evidence was mostly moderate or low due to methodological limitations, which prevented definitive conclusions. Both IMMA and oral miltefosine likely increase cure rates, but miltefosine is associated with higher rates of nausea and vomiting. Future research should focus on treatments for mucosal leishmaniasis, recurrence rates of cutaneous leishmaniasis, and its progression to mucosal disease.
